body:
## Learner promise
**We teach people to understand computers, make informed choices and create original games—not merely transcribe listings.** Learners should be able to predict, explain, modify, debug and independently create. Course completion is not proof of comprehension.

## Scope
Shared pseudocode Foundations (programming, numbers/bits, logic, maths for games), The Craft/game design, language/system pathways (BASIC, assembly, AMOS, Blitz BASIC), visual art and technical asset production, audio/music, debugging/profiling, tutorials, interactive examples and video. Assess accessibility, progression, clarity and actual learner outcomes.

## Quality obligations
- Every important objective has an appropriate demonstration of understanding: prediction, explanation, modification, debugging or transfer to a new problem.
- Reproducibly run technical examples in declared machine/tool configurations and record outcomes; relate to #65 without claiming internal emulator agreement is hardware proof.
- Art/graphics and sound/audio are first-class disciplines: composition, readability, asset creation, representations, conversion, animation, memory/timing costs, music, synthesis, sequencers, SFX, playback and creative direction.
- Capstone games define machine configuration, historically researched **system-specific era**, genre/scope, representative commercial benchmarks and required gameplay/control/art/audio/engineering polish. Differentiate what was technically possible, documented, typical and discovered later. Distinguish era-authentic output from modern tooling used to make it.
- Learners should create *their own* work, not just reproduce the supplied game. Include originality, playtesting, iteration and accessible alternatives.
- Video lessons share reviewed examples, objectives and versioned assets with the written/interactive pathways rather than becoming a disconnected second curriculum. Pilot before scaling.
- AI can investigate, draft and test but cannot alone establish educational effectiveness or historical truth. Use human editorial ownership and real learners.

## Approachability and progression gates

- Remove avoidable installation, hardware-cost and prior-knowledge barriers. Explain the machine's real memory, timing, language and media constraints as learners encounter them; accessible tooling must not hide the mechanism the lesson teaches.
- Keep learner agency central: offer meaningful route choices, inspectable examples and tasks that require explanation or a new decision. A runnable listing or AI-produced answer alone cannot establish understanding.
- Before extending a pilot, review technical execution, independent cross-tool checks, source accuracy, accessibility and real learner evidence separately. Record unavailable learner evidence honestly. Revise, withhold or cut weak material rather than scale it because it is easy to generate.
- Use the accountability and evidence gates in #108 and the scan/source checks in #109; retain the existing system-specific era and capstone contracts.

## First slices
- [ ] Foundations conceptual/progression and learner-understanding audit
- [ ] Spectrum BASIC and assembly pathway pilot
- [ ] Amiga AMOS and Blitz BASIC pathway pilot
- [ ] Graphics, technical assets and sound/music progression definition
- [ ] Era model and one commercial-quality capstone rubric/pilot
- [ ] One written + interactive + short video pilot with real learner feedback

Related: Vault provenance epic and Pattern Library qualification epic; #65 cross-stack qualification. Keep each child's completion specific and independently evidenced.
title: [Epic] Define and demonstrate exemplary Code198x learning and game-production quality
